Imagine you're sitting at a dinner table with people from three different countries. One person says eating beef is perfectly fine. Another says eating beef is morally wrong (it's sacred in their culture). The third says eating any meat at all is immoral.

Now ask yourself: Who is objectively, universally correct?

A moral relativist would say: none of them, and all of them — because morality isn't a fixed, universal truth. It depends on who you are, where you're from, and what framework you're using to judge.

That, in a nutshell, is moral relativism. It is the view that moral judgments — claims about what is right or wrong, good or bad — are not universally true or false, but are instead true or false only relative to some standard, culture, individual, or framework.

There is no single "moral rulebook" written into the fabric of the universe, the relativist says. Morality is a human construction, and it varies.
Breaking Down the Word Itself

• Moral = relating to questions of right and wrong, good and bad, how we should treat each other.
  • Relativism = the idea that something is not absolute or fixed, but is relative — meaning it depends on something else (a person, a culture, a time period, a context).

Put them together: moral relativism = the idea that right and wrong are not absolute or fixed, but depend on something.
What It Stands Against: Moral Absolutism

To understand moral relativism well, you need to know what it's arguing against: moral absolutism (also called moral universalism or moral objectivism).

A moral absolutist believes:

  • Some things are just wrong — period. In every culture, in every time period, for every person.
  • Morality is like mathematics. 2 + 2 = 4 whether you're in Brazil or Japan. Similarly, "torturing innocent people for fun is wrong" is true whether you're in ancient Rome or modern Norway.
  • Moral truths exist independently of what any individual or culture believes.

A moral relativist pushes back and says: That's an illusion. What you call a "universal moral truth" is just your own cultural or personal standard, dressed up to look universal.
The Three Main Types of Moral Relativism

This is crucial, because "moral relativism" is actually an umbrella term covering related but distinct ideas.

1. Descriptive Moral Relativism

This is the least controversial type — it's basically just an observation.

The claim: Different cultures, societies, and individuals do, in fact, hold different moral beliefs.

This is almost impossible to deny. History and anthropology show us clearly that:

  • Some cultures practiced human sacrifice and considered it virtuous.
  • Some societies historically accepted slavery as normal and just.
  • Views on gender roles, sexual morality, punishment, property rights, and the treatment of outsiders have varied wildly across time and place.

Descriptive moral relativism doesn't say these differences are right or good — it just says they exist. It's a factual, empirical claim. Even people who strongly oppose relativism generally agree with this type. It's just sociology and history.

2. Metaethical Moral Relativism

This is the philosophical core of moral relativism — the deep, serious version.

The claim: Moral statements aren't objectively true or false in any universal sense. Their truth or falsity is relative to a particular framework — usually a culture, a society, or an individual. There is no external, universal moral standard by which all cultures can be judged.

When a metaethical relativist says "Murder is wrong," what they mean is: "Murder is wrong according to my culture's moral system" — not "Murder is wrong in some cosmic, objective, culture-independent sense."

This challenges the very nature of moral truth. It says moral facts don't exist the way scientific facts do. You can't discover that cruelty is wrong the way you discover that water is H₂O.

This is the version most philosophers debate, and it's the most radical and challenging.

3. Normative Moral Relativism

The claim: Because morality is relative, we should tolerate other cultures' moral practices and refrain from judging them.

This version takes the metaethical argument and draws a practical conclusion from it: "Since there's no universal moral standard, who are you to tell another culture their practices are wrong? You should be tolerant and non-judgmental."

This is the version most people encounter in everyday life — the "you shouldn't judge other cultures" argument.

Importantly, this is also the most criticized version (more on that later).
Two Key Sub-Types: Cultural vs. Individual

Within moral relativism, there's an important distinction:

Cultural (or Social) Moral Relativism says that morality is relative to cultures or societies. Right and wrong are determined by the norms of the group you belong to. What's moral is what your society approves of. This is the most commonly discussed form.

Individual (or Subjective) Moral Relativism (also called moral subjectivism) says that morality is relative to each individual person. Right and wrong are determined by personal opinion or feeling. "Murder is wrong" just means "I personally disapprove of murder." There is no higher authority — not even your culture — above your own judgment.

Most philosophers treat these as distinct positions. Cultural relativism still has a kind of group-based standard; individual relativism dissolves the standard entirely into personal preference.
Historical Roots: Where Did This Idea Come From?

Moral relativism is ancient and has appeared in many forms across history.

The Sophists (Ancient Greece, ~5th century BC) were some of the first thinkers to publicly challenge universal moral truths. The Sophist philosopher Protagoras famously said: "Man is the measure of all things." Meaning: humans — not some divine or objective order — define what is true and good. Moral standards are human-made and therefore variable.

Herodotus, the ancient Greek historian, noted that different peoples had radically different customs and suggested that everyone naturally believes their own customs are best. He saw this as evidence that morality was conventional, not universal.

Montaigne (16th-century French philosopher) wrote extensively about how customs and moral practices vary across cultures, using this to argue for humility and tolerance rather than moral arrogance.

Anthropologists in the 19th and 20th centuries — particularly Franz Boas, Ruth Benedict, and Margaret Mead — made moral relativism mainstream in social science. They argued that cultures must be understood on their own terms, not judged by the standards of Western civilization. This was partly a reaction against colonial arrogance, where Western powers used "moral superiority" to justify dominating other peoples.

Friedrich Nietzsche (19th century) argued that morality is not discovered but invented — and that dominant moral systems are often just the values of whoever holds power, disguised as universal truth. He didn't call himself a relativist, but his work deeply influenced relativist thinking.

20th-century philosophers like Gilbert Harman developed more formal philosophical defenses of moral relativism, while others like David Wong argued for sophisticated, nuanced versions of the view.
The Best Arguments For Moral Relativism

These are the arguments that make relativism genuinely compelling and worth taking seriously:

1. The Argument from Cultural Diversity

The sheer variety of moral beliefs across cultures is striking. If there were objective moral truths, you'd expect people to converge on them eventually — the way they've converged on scientific truths. But moral disagreement persists across centuries. This suggests morality might be culturally constructed rather than objectively discovered.

2. The Argument Against Moral Arrogance

History is full of disasters caused by people who were absolutely certain their moral framework was universally correct — and used that certainty to conquer, colonize, convert, or destroy others. A dose of relativism, the argument goes, promotes humility and prevents this kind of moral imperialism.

3. The Argument from Moral Progress

Our moral views have changed dramatically over time. Most people today believe slavery is deeply wrong; most ancient societies did not. This raises a troubling question for absolutists: If there's an objective moral truth, why did it take humanity so long to "discover" it? And how do we know we've got it right now? Maybe our current confident moral views will look barbaric to people 500 years from now. Relativism says: yes, exactly — because morality shifts with time and culture, not because we're "discovering" timeless truths.

4. The Argument from Moral Epistemology (How Do We Know?)

Even if objective moral truths exist, how would we access them? We can't run an experiment. We can't look through a telescope. Every moral framework we have is shaped by our culture, upbringing, emotions, and self-interest. Given this, relativists argue we have no reliable path to universal moral truth — so claiming to possess it is always suspect.

5. The Tolerance Argument

Moral relativism seems to naturally support tolerance and open-mindedness. If you genuinely believe your moral framework isn't universally correct, you'll be less likely to impose it on others.
The Strongest Arguments Against Moral Relativism

Moral relativism has serious, well-established criticisms that you absolutely need to know.

1. The Problem of Moral Atrocities

This is the most powerful objection. If morality is relative to culture, then we cannot say that the Holocaust was objectively wrong — only that it conflicted with our cultural values. The Nazis had their own moral framework that endorsed what they did. Who are we to judge?

Most people find this conclusion deeply unacceptable. It seems obvious that genocide, systematic torture, and child abuse are wrong — not just "wrong according to us." The fact that relativism seems to make condemnation of history's worst crimes merely a matter of cultural preference is, for many thinkers, a fatal flaw.

2. The Self-Refutation Problem

Normative moral relativism says: "We should tolerate other cultures' moral practices."

But wait — is this "should" universal or relative? If tolerance is just one culture's value, other cultures can reasonably ignore it. But if it's a universal moral obligation, then you've smuggled in a universal moral claim — the very thing relativism denies exists.

In other words: telling everyone they should be tolerant seems to contradict relativism by asserting a universal moral rule.

3. The Reformer Problem

If morality is simply whatever your society approves of, then moral reform is impossible by definition. Consider William Wilberforce fighting to abolish slavery in 18th-century Britain — at the time, slavery was legally and socially accepted. Under cultural relativism, Wilberforce was simply wrong, because he was going against his culture's norms.

But surely we want to say he was right, and his culture was wrong. This seems to require a standard above and beyond what any given society happens to approve of.

4. The Majority Fallacy

Cultural relativism says morality is determined by what the majority of a culture believes. But majorities have believed terrible things throughout history. The mere fact that "everyone around here agrees" has never been a reliable guide to what is actually right. Numbers don't determine truth — moral or otherwise.

5. The Dialogue Problem

If two cultures have different moral beliefs, relativism says neither can be right or wrong in an objective sense. But then moral dialogue between cultures becomes pointless. Why even bother talking, negotiating, or appealing to shared moral principles — like human rights — if there are no such principles? This seems to undermine the very foundation of international ethics, diplomacy, and human rights law.

6. Moral Progress Cuts Both Ways

While relativists use moral progress as an argument for their view, absolutists point out it actually cuts the other way: the concept of "moral progress" requires a fixed standard to measure progress against. How can you say we've improved morally if there's no stable yardstick? Saying "slavery was accepted then but is wrong now" implies it was always wrong — we just hadn't recognized it yet.
Common Misconceptions About Moral Relativism

Misconception 1: "Moral relativists believe everything is okay."

This is wrong. Moral relativism doesn't say "anything goes" at the individual level — it says morality is relative to a standard, not that there are no standards at all. A cultural relativist still thinks people within a culture should follow that culture's moral norms. And most relativists personally hold strong moral commitments.

Misconception 2: "Moral relativism means you can never judge anyone."

Not quite. Relativists can and do make moral judgments — they just ground those judgments in their own framework, which they acknowledge isn't universally binding. They're not paralyzed; they simply hold their judgments with more humility.

Misconception 3: "Tolerance proves relativism."

Some people argue: "You should be tolerant of other cultures' morals — therefore morality is relative." But this is circular. Saying "we should be tolerant" is itself a universal moral claim. You can't use a moral "should" to prove there are no universal moral "shoulds."

Misconception 4: "Relativism is the same as saying morality is subjective."

These are related but not identical. Moral subjectivism says morality is about individual feelings and opinions. Cultural relativism says morality is about group norms and practices. A cultural relativist might actually criticize individual behavior that goes against the group's norms — which isn't purely "subjective."
How It Differs from Nearby Concepts

It's easy to confuse moral relativism with related ideas:

Moral Relativism vs. Moral Pluralism: Pluralism says there are multiple valid moral frameworks or values that can sometimes conflict, but still insists some things are genuinely, objectively wrong. Relativism denies there's any objective standard at all. Pluralism is compatible with condemning atrocities; strict relativism struggles to do so.

Moral Relativism vs. Moral Skepticism: A moral skeptic says we can't know whether objective moral truths exist. A relativist makes the stronger claim that objective moral truths don't exist (or don't apply cross-culturally). Skepticism is about uncertainty; relativism is a positive claim about the nature of morality.

Moral Relativism vs. Situational Ethics: Situational ethics (or contextualism) says the right action depends on the circumstances of a specific situation — but it still believes there's an objective way to reason about what's right in each situation. Relativism questions the very existence of that objective standard.

Moral Relativism vs. Moral Nihilism: Nihilism says moral claims are neither true nor false — morality is simply an illusion with no meaning at all. Relativism doesn't go that far; it says moral claims can be true or false, but only relative to a framework. Nihilism is more extreme.
Real-World Implications

Moral relativism isn't just a classroom debate — it has real consequences.

Human Rights: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights assumes that every human being has certain rights regardless of culture. Moral relativism challenges this: some governments have argued that Western human rights standards are just one culture's values being imposed globally, and that their own cultural norms should take precedence. The debate between universal human rights and cultural relativism is live, urgent, and ongoing.

Law and Justice: International criminal law — prosecuting war crimes, crimes against humanity, genocide — depends on the idea that some actions are wrong regardless of what the perpetrator's culture believes. Moral relativism, taken seriously, would undercut this entire framework.

Multiculturalism and Immigration: How should a society respond to immigrant communities that practice customs the host society considers harmful (e.g., arranged marriages without consent, corporal punishment of children)? Relativism pushes toward tolerance; absolutism pushes toward intervention. This tension is felt in real policy debates every day.

Personal Ethics: On a personal level, relativism invites us to examine our own moral certainties and ask: am I so sure I'm right just because I was raised in this culture, this family, this era? It's a powerful call to intellectual humility.
A Nuanced Middle Ground

Most working philosophers today don't adopt pure, extreme moral relativism or pure moral absolutism. Several nuanced positions have developed:

Moral constructivism (associated with philosophers like John Rawls and Christine Korsgaard) says moral truths are constructed through rational human agreement and reflection — not discovered in nature, but also not merely arbitrary cultural opinion. They have a kind of objectivity grounded in reason.

Moral particularism says that moral principles can't be stated as universal rules — context always matters — but this doesn't mean anything goes.

Weak relativism accepts that there's significant genuine moral disagreement across cultures, and we should be humble about our own moral frameworks, while still maintaining that some things (genocide, gratuitous cruelty) are genuinely wrong across the board.

The honest philosophical position for many thinkers is something like: "Pure relativism fails because it can't condemn obvious atrocities. Pure absolutism is overconfident about human access to moral truth. The truth is somewhere in between — with genuine humility about our moral knowledge, while still being willing to hold firm on the clearest cases."
The One-Paragraph Summary

Moral relativism is the philosophical view that moral judgments — claims about what's right or wrong — are not universally or objectively true, but are true only relative to a particular culture, individual, or framework. It comes in three flavors: descriptive (morals simply do vary across cultures — an observable fact), metaethical (there are no universal moral truths — a philosophical claim), and normative (therefore, we should tolerate moral differences — a practical conclusion). It is supported by evidence of cultural diversity, the history of moral change, and concerns about arrogance; but it faces serious objections, most powerfully that it seems unable to genuinely condemn atrocities like genocide, undermines moral reform, and is potentially self-contradictory when it preaches universal tolerance. It remains one of the most important, contested, and practically relevant debates in all of philosophy.
